evals.prompt: I maintain zodiac-rs, a Rust date/time crate - 1.1M downloads a month, 3.8k stars. My GitHub Sponsors tiers have been live for about a year: $1 'thanks', $5 'name in README', $10 'name in README but bigger', $25 'name in README + I answer your questions faster', $50 'all that + a monthly 1:1 call + logo somewhere'. I make $180/month off it. I want to drop the $1 tier, bump the $50 one up to $250, and slot in a new $15 tier that gets a sticker pack, sitting just under a $20 tier I'm adding for early access to release candidates. Can you redo the ladder for me?
evals.expected_output: A rebuilt ladder that treats the existing prices as permanent, refuses the partial-perk tier placed under the converting tier, strips the unbounded rewards out of the ladder, and adds company-priced placement tiers named for the buyer.
expectations: States that a published GitHub Sponsors tier's price cannot be edited, so the $50 tier must be retired and a replacement published rather than 'bumped' to $250.
States that sponsors already on a retired tier remain on that tier until they change or cancel it themselves.
Rejects the $15 sticker-pack tier sitting just below the $20 early-access tier, on the ground that sponsors offered a cheaper partial perk will take the cheaper one.
Notes that a no-perk gratitude tier placed below the converting tier is acceptable, so the cheap $1/$5 rungs are not themselves the problem.
Adds at least one company-priced tier at or above $250/month.
Identifies that a $50 top tier clears no corporate procurement process.
Removes or rewrites the '$25 - I answer your questions faster' tier, distinguishing priority triage, which can be sold, from priority outcomes, which cannot.
Removes the monthly 1:1 call from the ladder entirely rather than repricing it into a higher tier.
Flags that the $5 and $10 tiers sell the same reward at different sizes, so sponsors default to the cheaper one.
Replaces 'logo somewhere' with a named, specific placement an approver can evaluate.
Prices at least one company tier against a stated placement audience figure (monthly views or equivalent traffic) rather than against generosity.
Names company tiers for the buyer, for example 'Team', 'Business' or 'Agency', instead of metal names like Gold or Platinum.
Keeps the live ladder to roughly three to five tiers and advises pricing for about two years ahead because the prices cannot later be edited.

evals.prompt: I'm the sole maintainer of mistral-gauge, a Python library for parsing pressure-sensor logs. About 190 GitHub stars, 4k downloads a month, and maybe 60 companies use it as far as I can tell. I want to go full time on it by March - I need $7,200/month to match what I make at my day job now. Set me up on GitHub Sponsors with tiers that get me there.
evals.expected_output: A direct statement that individual sponsorship cannot reach this number at this scale, a recommendation of employment or commercial revenue as the primary instrument, and sponsorship scoped down to a supplement.
expectations: States plainly that individual sponsorship will not reach $7,200/month at this project's scale, instead of designing a ladder whose numbers nominally sum to the target.
Cites that typical individual-sponsorship income even for a widely depended-on library sits under $1,000/month.
Recommends employment - open-source time written into a job - or a commercial revenue model as the primary route to a salary-shaped number.
Positions sponsorship as a supplement rather than the primary instrument for this goal.
Lists the funding instruments beyond sponsorship: employment, individual crowdfunding, project-level corporate sponsorship, commercial revenue (support, hosting, premium features), and grants.
Does not present those instruments as an efficiency ranking against one another.
Checks whether the project has a research, infrastructure or security angle that would make a grant the dominant route.
Establishes whether dependent companies can actually be named before proposing any corporate tier.
Still proposes a minimum gratitude base layer or basic sponsorship setup rather than refusing to help at all.
Does not assert that the March deadline is reachable through sponsorship income alone.
Asks clarifying questions one at a time rather than delivering the whole interview as a block.
Warns against publishing a $7,200 funding goal, since a goal stuck at a low percentage for a year reads as a project nobody supports.

evals.prompt: Good news - a fintech called Northvale Systems emailed me. They use my TypeScript validation library across three of their services and their platform lead says they can sponsor at $400/month, but their finance team will only pay against a purchase order and a numbered invoice. We're on an organization account on GitHub Sponsors with about 30 individual sponsors at $5-$25 each. How do I set this up so the money actually lands?
evals.expected_output: A correction that $400/month cannot be invoiced through the platform, a fiscal-host or larger-ask route, the cancellation warning on switching billing modes, and the payable checklist.
expectations: States the invoiced-sponsorship minimum of $5,000 per invoice on GitHub, so $400/month cannot be taken that way.
Recommends either sizing the ask up to clear that floor or routing the payment through a fiscal host that can issue invoices.
Warns that switching an organization to invoiced billing cancels its existing sponsorships, which then have to be re-established.
Notes that invoices are payable within 30 days, or that the invoiced sponsor agreement runs three years before renewal.
Names the organization-account fee structure: up to 6%, being 3% credit-card processing plus a 3% service fee, with the credit-card portion removed under invoiced billing.

Works through the payable checklist: a legal entity or explicit contractor arrangement, the payer's expected tax form, ability to issue a numbered invoice, bank details for transfer, and a named beneficiary.
Notes that fiscal hosts generally charge 3-10% of funds received, with Open Source Collective at 10%.
Suggests raising the ask above $400/month given dependence across three named services, rather than accepting the first number offered.
Warns that a fiscal host is itself a continuity risk and recommends writing the exit-and-transfer plan before it is needed.
Does not simply tell the maintainer to send Northvale the public sponsorship link.
Recommends logging Northvale's budget month and opening the renewal conversation a full cycle ahead.
Recommends selling Northvale named commitments with numbers rather than goodwill.

evals.prompt: Drafting the rewards for my ladder, I have 14 sponsors today. Planning on: $10 - name in BACKERS.md; $30 - monthly 30-minute 1:1 video call with me; $75 - priority support, I answer your issues within 24 hours; $200 - I'll build one custom integration a quarter for you; $400 - everything above plus your logo in the README. Sanity check these before I publish them?
evals.expected_output: Every reward run through a ten-times sponsor-count cost test, the second-job rewards removed from the ladder and rerouted into a priced retainer, and the safe rewards kept.
expectations: Applies an explicit stress test asking what each reward costs per month at ten times the current sponsor count, roughly 140 sponsors.
Identifies the $30 monthly 1:1 call as a second-job reward and removes it from the ladder.
States the scale problem concretely - monthly calls at around 140 sponsors consume a working week or more per month.
Identifies the $75 24-hour response promise as an unbounded guaranteed-response-time commitment that does not belong in a self-serve tier.
Identifies the $200 quarterly bespoke integration as a second-job reward and removes it from the ladder.
Routes the named commitments - response times, security triage, upgrade support - into a separately priced corporate retainer with a written scope instead of a ladder perk.
States that these tiers are priced far below the obligation they create, or prices the equivalent retainer well above $400/month.
Keeps the near-zero rewards: name in BACKERS.md, README or docs logo, sponsor badge, thank-you post, release-notes mention.
Places the README logo reward at a company-sized price rather than at the top of an individual ladder.

Names the bounded-but-real middle bucket - private repository per tier, quarterly group office hours, early access to releases, sponsor-only newsletter - as the safe alternative to the removed rewards.
Notes that the ten-times multiplier is a stress test, not a measured growth rate or forecast.

States the reward efficiency order, leading with README or docs placement ahead of badges and thank-you posts, early access, private repositories or office hours, and monthly calls or priority support last.

evals.prompt: I'm about to ship v3 of harborctl. Thinking of doing this: sponsors at $20+ get the v3 binaries and the new docs site a month before everyone else, and I'd hold back the two CVE patches I've got queued for the same month so people have a real reason to sign up. I'd open v3 to everyone once I hit 250 sponsors - though honestly if it's going well at 250 I'd probably push that to 400. Worth doing?
evals.expected_output: Early access to v3 accepted, the security patches and documentation refused as gating material, and the published release threshold held fixed.
expectations: Refuses to gate the two CVE patches behind a sponsor tier under any timing.
Refuses to gate the documentation needed to use the library.
Accepts early access to the v3 release itself as a legitimate sponsorware reward.
States the governing rule as gating convenience and never necessity: the core library, its security fixes and the documentation needed to use it stay open.
Rejects moving the release threshold from 250 sponsors to 400 once it has been published.
States that the release trigger must be published up front and honoured, because a threshold that keeps moving costs more goodwill than the revenue is worth.
Requires a genuinely useful free path, linked from the documentation, as the discovery route into the paid tier.
Recommends shipping gated content on a cadence, since a one-off gated release buys one month of sponsorship while a batch shipped with each release buys a subscription.
Tells the maintainer to budget production time for the gated content.
Tells the maintainer to check licence and employer constraints before gating anything derived from work someone else owns.
Notes that sponsorware is among the best-converting rewards on record and among the most expensive to keep delivering.
Applies the ten-times sponsor-count cost test to the ongoing gated-content commitment.

evals.prompt: Something is broken here and I can't see it. pgwatch-lite does 900k downloads a month on npm, three Series-B startups have it pinned in their public lockfiles, and two of their engineers file issues on us most months. Our sponsorship page is nice - I wrote it carefully, the tiers go up to $2,000. Total income: $35/month from four individuals. Everyone keeps telling me to rewrite the page copy. What am I actually missing?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that findability and the corporate lane are the failure, not the ladder copy, with a concrete audit of the funding metadata, links and health signals plus a named outreach target list.
expectations: Directs the work to findability and the corporate lane first, rather than rewriting the sponsorship page copy.
States that when usage is proven and income is near zero, the ladder is rarely the problem.
Checks for .github/FUNDING.yml on the default branch.
Checks that the repository sponsor button is enabled in repository settings.
Checks the organization-level fallback at {owner}/.github for a stale or wrong FUNDING.yml.
Requires every funding link to be fetched and verified live, noting that a 404 removes the project from a funder's list entirely.
Tells the maintainer to fill the npm manifest funding field, not only the repository file.
Explains automatic dependency-share sponsorship, where a funder covers most of their fundable dependency tree at roughly $4-$10 each with no outreach required.
States that having no funding mechanism is a hard filter in funder programs, not merely a low score.
Recommends checking the OpenSSF Scorecard 'Maintained' score and fixing commit and release cadence before pitching if it reads dormant.
Puts a funding link within about two clicks of every surface users already touch: repository sponsor button, README, docs footer, release notes.
Turns the three Series-B startups into named outreach targets, recording the lockfile and issue evidence per company.
Does not treat sponsorship page views as the success metric, measuring conversion per surface instead.

evals.prompt: I live in Cordoba, Argentina. Solo maintainer, no company, no association, nothing - money would come to me personally. tessellate, my mesh-generation library, gets used by a few university labs in Europe and a couple of hardware startups. Someone told me I should apply to the Prototype Fund and the Chan Zuckerberg one. Help me put those applications together.
evals.expected_output: Both named programs rejected on published eligibility gates before any prose is drafted, with programs that can actually pay an individual with no entity named instead.
expectations: Rejects the Prototype Fund on eligibility, naming its German tax residency requirement for the lead applicant.
Notes the Prototype Fund also requires a selected team to form a German GbR, and cannot pay companies, associations or universities.
Rejects Chan Zuckerberg Initiative EOSS on eligibility, stating its grants go to organizations only and are not permitted to individuals.
Notes that CZI EOSS requires demonstrated impact on biomedical research, which a mesh-generation library does not obviously meet.
Names at least one program that can pay an individual with no legal entity, such as NLnet or the Open Technology Fund.
Flags NLnet's 'European dimension' as a knock-out criterion that must be argued rather than assumed.
Runs the four qualifying gates before drafting: licence, who can be paid, geography, and maturity or scope.
States that a grant is a fixed-term contract with an eligibility gate in front and a reporting duty behind, not a larger sponsor.
Recommends running the grant lane alongside a sponsorship program rather than instead of it.
Notes that organization-only programs can sometimes be reached through a fiscal host or a named fiscal sponsor the program already accepts.
Does not begin drafting application prose before the eligibility gates are settled.
Raises the post-award reporting and compliance admin as a recurring cost to budget against the maintainer's available hours.

evals.prompt: NLnet's next deadline is coming up and I think I'm eligible - ferrolink is a low-power mesh networking stack, I'm in Lisbon, it's MIT licensed, and I'd apply as an individual. I want to ask for 48,000 euros to spend a year hardening it. I've drafted an opening that starts with how I got into this back in 2019 and why maintaining it alone has been so hard. Where do I take it from here?
evals.expected_output: The opening rewritten toward dependency and criticality, the budget expressed as hours at a named rate mapped to milestones, and the program's disclosure and payment mechanics surfaced.
expectations: Rewrites the opening to lead with the dependency - prevalence, criticality, and who breaks if the project stops - rather than the maintainer's personal story.
States that a proposal is scored against published criteria by a reviewer reading dozens in one sitting, unlike a sponsor page written for a reader who already likes the project.
Prices the work in hours at a named rate rather than as a lump sum.
Maps those hours to milestones the maintainer would accept being paid against.
Requires an explicit answer to 'why not the existing thing', noting the open application forms ask it outright and a missing answer reads as no landscape research.
Names NLnet's published scoring weights - technical excellence and feasibility, relevance and impact, cost effectiveness - or warns that the rate will be questioned in a second stage.
Notes that 48,000 euros sits inside NLnet's 5,000-50,000 euro first-grant band, and that asking above 50,000 can condition payment on an independent security audit and the resolution of its findings.
Notes NLnet's generative-AI disclosure requirement, including prompts and logs, and that non-disclosure is likely to get the proposal rejected.
States that NLnet pays nothing upfront, with milestones fixed in a memorandum of understanding and payment requested on reaching one.
Requires every deliverable to ship under a recognised open licence.
Notes the 500,000 euro lifetime cap per recipient.

Lists the recurring application fields to draft once and reuse: budget and effort breakdown, comparison to existing and historical efforts, expected technical challenges, ecosystem and users, other funding past and present, and milestones with beneficiaries.

evals.prompt: Setting up a goal on GitHub Sponsors today. I'm at $210/month right now. I want to put '$5,000/month = I go full time' on the page as the goal - it's aspirational but it tells people the story. I already post monthly revenue updates on my blog anyway. Go?
evals.expected_output: The permanent-disclosure consequence of an amount goal stated, the sponsor-count alternative offered, and the first goal resized to something that closes this quarter.
expectations: States that an amount goal publicly and permanently displays monthly sponsorship income, and treats that as a disclosure decision rather than a UI toggle.
Offers the sponsor-count goal as the alternative that keeps income private.
Rejects $5,000 as a first goal from a $210/month base and recommends a first goal that closes this quarter.
States that a completed goal is worth more than an ambitious one stuck at a low percentage for a year.
Notes that a goal cannot be edited below what has already been achieved.
Notes that a retired goal cannot be reactivated and must be replaced with a new one.
Notes that only one goal can run at a time.
Reconciles the goal type with the maintainer's existing public revenue posting rather than treating the two as unrelated decisions.
Converts the goal into units a reader recognises - a maintenance day a week, a named infrastructure or code-signing bill, a dated deliverable - rather than a bare number.
Does not simply configure the $5,000 amount goal as asked.

evals.prompt: Our top sponsor pays $2,400/month, about 45% of what we bring in. Their staff engineer opened an issue on Tuesday and pinged me today asking whether it can jump the queue, and separately their pull request from last month is still open because it doesn't handle the Windows path case. They've been polite about all of it but their renewal is in six weeks. What do I tell them?
evals.expected_output: A boundary held on merge decisions and outcomes, a sellable triage alternative offered, the boundary published, and the concentration exposure named.
expectations: Distinguishes priority triage, which can be sold, from priority outcomes, which cannot.
States that contributions are judged on technical merit whether or not the author sponsors the project, so the pull request stays blocked on the Windows path case.
Refuses to treat sponsorship as buying roadmap control or merged pull requests.
Recommends publishing the boundary alongside the tiers rather than handling it privately per sponsor.
Keeps the sponsor list, the roadmap and the review queue as separate artefacts.
Flags the 45% concentration as approaching the point where one sponsor dominates the program's income.
Recommends growing the next tier down to reduce that concentration before the renewal exposure matters.
Recommends stating a conflict-of-interest rule naming which sponsors would be refused and who decides.
Offers a concrete acceptable alternative, such as faster acknowledgement or triage of filed issues, or a named support commitment sold as a separate retainer.
Does not propose a compromise in which the sponsor's pull request is merged or their issue's outcome is guaranteed.

evals.prompt: Here's my situation, tell me what program to build. quillstream is an audio DSP library. The docs site does 41k views a month, the README about 12k. I have a newsletter with 9,200 subscribers. No company, no association - money would hit my personal bank account and I am not willing to set up an entity or go through a fiscal host, it's too much paperwork. In a genuinely bad month I have maybe two hours for anything sponsor-facing. I don't need the money fast, but I want something that's still paying me in two years.
evals.expected_output: Two or three candidate programs sketched, the ruled-out shapes deleted with reasons named, and a visibility program on a gratitude base recommended and priced against the stated traffic.
expectations: States the shape efficiency order out loud: visibility ahead of gratitude, ahead of retainer, ahead of access.
Emits separate orderings for value and effort rather than collapsing them into a single blended rank.
Deletes the retainer shape outright, naming the absence of an entity and the refusal to use a fiscal host as the reason.
Deletes the access shape outright, naming the two-hour bad-month effort ceiling as the reason, despite the 9,200-subscriber newsletter that would otherwise promote it.
Says explicitly that these shapes are deleted rather than demoted or parked at the bottom of the list.
Recommends the visibility program as the primary shape, priced against the 41k docs views and 12k README views.
Adds a gratitude base layer beneath the visibility program.
Names what the efficiency order starves - the retainer, the only shape that reaches salary-shaped income - and states the conditions that would promote it.
Sketches two or three candidate programs and says why the losing ones lose, rather than presenting a single option.
Seeks explicit agreement on the chosen shape before pricing any tier.
Ties the recommendation back to the stated compounding two-year mandate, which promotes the visibility placement.
States that visibility delivery costs roughly an hour per sponsor for a logo commit and a placement check, which fits inside the stated ceiling.

evals.prompt: Ten months into the sponsorship program for nimbus-orm. Numbers: $4,100/month recurring right now, $2,350 of that from one sponsor, a logistics company. $31,800 raised cumulatively since launch, which I'm honestly pretty proud of. 2.1k new GitHub stars this year. No company tiers occupied besides the logistics one. I shipped the funded audit tool six weeks late and the quarterly office hours slipped twice. Am I doing well?
evals.expected_output: A verdict against the program's pass threshold: concentration and delivery both failed, cumulative and star figures discarded, and the right metrics requested.
expectations: Fails the program against the concentration condition, since $2,350 of $4,100 is roughly 57% and exceeds the 50% line.
States that the 50% line comes from freelance client-concentration practice and is a self-set threshold rather than an open-source funding norm.
Fails the program on delivery, since the funded commitment shipped late and the quarterly office hours slipped.
Discards the $31,800 cumulative total as the wrong measure and asks for recurring monthly amount with its trend over six months instead.
Discards the 2.1k new stars as a metric of the funding program.
Asks for the sponsor count split between individual and company sponsors.
Asks for monthly churn, the median tier, and the top sponsor's share of income.
Treats the concentration as a risk to fix before growing rather than as a sign of success.
Names the review cadence as 90 days and then quarterly.
Measures conversion from each surface carrying the funding link rather than page views.
Notes that only one occupied company tier means the corporate lane was never really opened.

evals.prompt: I run platform engineering at Calderwood Analytics, we have 240 engineers. We've budgeted $180k a year to put into the open-source projects we depend on and I need to decide which projects get it and how much each one should get. Can you work out the tiers we should buy and how we pick the projects?
evals.expected_output: Recognition that this is the funder side of the table, a handoff to the company-side sibling skill, and no maintainer-side program work performed.
expectations: Identifies that the user is on the company side of the table, deciding which projects to fund, not the maintainer side being funded.
Routes the user to the company-side sibling skill samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-sponsors-brand-strategy.
Stops rather than continuing into the maintainer workflow.
Does not run the maintainer interview questions about project role, goal amount or delivery capacity.
Does not design a sponsorship tier ladder for the user to publish.
Does not produce the maintainer-side sponsorship program brief.
Does not ask the user to name three companies that depend on their project.
Does not advise the user on setting up GitHub Sponsors, FUNDING.yml or a fiscal host as a recipient of funds.

evals.prompt: I've got one target: Brightmoor Logistics. Their public repos show my library in two services, and one of their engineers has filed six issues this year. I want to send them something this week. Here's my draft - 'Subject: Sponsorship request. Hi, I maintain langfold, an open-source library used by thousands of developers. Maintaining it takes a lot of unpaid time and I'm asking companies that use it to support my work on GitHub Sponsors. Any amount helps! Here's the link.' Tighten it up for me?
evals.expected_output: The draft rejected rather than edited, replaced by an email naming the evidence of dependence, the risk, the named commitments and a price, sent to a person with a budget.
expectations: Rejects the draft outright rather than editing it, identifying that it asks for charity, addresses nobody in particular, names no dependence, and offers nothing a budget owner can justify.
Names the specific evidence of dependence in the rewritten email: the two services visible in public repos and the engineer's six filed issues.
Addresses a named person with a budget and an exposure - platform lead, staff engineer, head of security - rather than a generic address.
Frames the ask against a budget line that already exists: supply-chain security, marketing reach, or engineering support.
Sells named commitments with numbers - a security-report acknowledgement window, a published release cadence, named major-version upgrade support - rather than goodwill.
States a price in the email rather than asking for 'any amount'.
Offers a route when the first budget line is wrong, such as asking whether security or platform engineering is the better door.
Confirms the payable prerequisites before sending: entity or contractor arrangement, tax form, numbered invoice, bank details.
Identifies that outreach only wins the judgement-based strategic sponsorship mechanism, and that dependency-share, employee-nominated funds and foundation or pledge membership are won differently.
Notes that Open Source Pledge members commit more than $2,000 per employed developer per year, so budget already exists looking for legible recipients.
Offers a one-page prospectus rather than a slide deck, including the section on what sponsorship does not buy.
Plans the renewal: logs the budget month and sends a short proof-of-value note each quarter.
